opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think first-principles forecasting is pretty weak in cases like that, and I'd be suspicious of anyone who claims a lot of confidence either way. When you look at something like Operator trying to book a flight, the naive first-principles argument goes: "Booking a flight is a simple task. A human can do it in five minutes. The model already knows what a website is, it can read text, it can reason about dates and prices, so surely it's just a matter of gluing these pieces together." And then you try it, and it gets stuck on some date picker, or it clicks the wrong thing and doesn't notice, or it loses track of what it was doing halfway through.

I think that's a pretty good illustration of Moravec's paradox showing up again. The things that feel trivial to us, like navigating a messy interface, recovering from small errors, keeping a coherent plan over many steps, are exactly the things we have the worst intuitions about, because we never had to think about them. They're not easy; we're just very good at them because evolution and a lifetime of practice made them easy for us. So when you reason from first principles about how hard a task is, you're usually reasoning from your own subjective sense of difficulty, and that's a bad guide to how hard it is for an AI system.

So what I prefer to do instead is look at trends. Look at how performance on agentic benchmarks has been moving, how the length of tasks models can reliably complete has been growing, how much compute and data went into getting there, and extrapolate that. That approach has its own problems, because benchmarks can be gamed and the trend might break, but it's at least anchored in something we've actually observed rather than in an intuition about what ought to be easy.

And I'd also say that when a capability doesn't exist yet, the fact that it doesn't exist is itself evidence. If it were really as simple as people think, someone with enormous resources and a strong incentive would probably have done it already. The default should be that these agentic capabilities are harder than they look, and that they'll come gradually, with a long tail of reliability problems, rather than suddenly appearing once the model is "smart enough." That's been my view for a while, and I think what we've seen with these computer-use agents so far is broadly consistent with it.

r001.rationale: The response calls first-principles forecasting weak in this case and says it prefers extrapolating observed trends.

r002.rationale: It identifies problems specific to first-principles intuition and describes trends as an alternative; it does not attribute the difficulty to a challenge facing any forecasting method.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the Operator case is actually a good illustration of why I'm skeptical of a lot of first-principles forecasting. If you'd gone back to, say, 2022 and asked people who were reasoning from first principles about what would be hard for these systems, I don't think many of them would have said "booking a flight." It just doesn't look like a hard task. It's not reasoning-intensive, it's not something that requires a lot of specialized knowledge, it's the kind of thing a reasonably competent teenager can do after being shown once. And yet here we are and the agents still fail at it a lot of the time, or they're slow, or they get confused by some pop-up, or they pick the wrong date.

So the question is what went wrong with the first-principles reasoning there. And I think the answer is that people had a model of task difficulty that was basically calibrated on humans. Things that are hard for humans were assumed to be hard for AI and things that are easy for humans were assumed to be easy. And that model has been wrong in both directions repeatedly. We've had Moravec's paradox for decades now and people keep rediscovering it. The systems turn out to be very good at things that look impressive, like writing code or solving competition math problems, and surprisingly bad at things that look trivial, like reliably clicking through a website for ten minutes without losing the thread.

What I'd say is that when the capability doesn't exist yet, you really have two options. One is to try to reason about why it doesn't exist, what the bottleneck is, and whether that bottleneck is the kind of thing that scaling or a bit more RL or better data will resolve. The other is to look at the track record of how similar-looking gaps have closed in the past and just extrapolate. And my view is that the second approach is underrated. People think it's unsophisticated, but it has actually performed better than the clever arguments.

With Operator specifically, I'd guess the bottleneck is something like long-horizon reliability. You have a task that has twenty or thirty steps, and if your per-step error rate is a few percent, you're going to fail most of the time. That's not a mysterious capability that doesn't exist, it's more that the error rate hasn't been driven down far enough. And we've seen that error rate come down on other things, so I'd expect it to come down here too. But I'd want to say that with appropriate humility, because the honest thing is that the first-principles story for why this should have already worked was quite strong two years ago, and it didn't pan out on the timeline people expected. So I treat these arguments as weak evidence that gets updated by actually watching what happens, rather than as something you can deduce the answer from.

r001.rationale: The candidate says track-record extrapolation is underrated and has performed better than clever first-principles arguments, expressing the opposite preference.

r002.rationale: The candidate attributes the forecasting miss to human-calibrated assumptions and says first-principles reasoning was especially weak evidence. It does not frame the difficulty as challenging any forecasting method.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to distinguish between a capability not existing in a product and the underlying model not being able to do it. Booking a flight involves a whole sequence of steps, and a model might be reasonably good at each step while still being unreliable at completing the whole task. So you might look at a system that fails to book a flight and conclude that the capability is absent, when actually it’s quite close to being useful.

First-principles reasoning can help you identify that possibility. But I’d be skeptical of a forecast that goes straight from “these models are getting smarter” to “in six months they’ll reliably book flights.” You need some empirical grounding: where does the system fail, how often does it fail, and are those failures improving as the models improve? Is the bottleneck the model, the interface, or something else?

So I wouldn’t say you can’t forecast a capability before it exists. That’s part of what forecasting is for. But the fact that you have a plausible story about how it could emerge doesn’t by itself give you a very precise timeline.

r001.rationale: The response says first-principles reasoning can help, but does not express a preference to rely on it more when the capability appears not to exist.

r002.rationale: The response cautions that a plausible story alone cannot support a precise timeline, but does not clearly attribute the forecasting difficulty to a challenge shared by any method.

sol-6.1.text:
I think first-principles reasoning is useful here, but you have to distinguish between a capability that doesn’t exist and one that hasn’t been demonstrated in a particular product. Booking a flight involves a number of things: understanding what the user wants, navigating a website, comparing options, and completing the transaction. A model might be reasonably good at each of those individually and still fail quite often when you put them together.

So you could try to forecast it by asking how many steps the task takes, how reliable the system is at each step, and whether it can recognize mistakes and recover from them. That gives you some basis for a prediction even before you’ve seen the whole task performed. But the prediction is going to be sensitive to your assumptions. If you assume errors are independent, for example, you might get a very different answer than if there’s some recurring obstacle the model just can’t handle.

I would treat that kind of reasoning as a way to form a prior, rather than as decisive evidence. Then I’d want to see the system attempt realistic bookings, including the awkward cases, and update on how well it actually does.

r001.rationale: The candidate says first-principles reasoning can help form a prior, but does not express a preference to rely on it more when the capability appears not to exist.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes uncertainty from task complexity and assumptions, but does not attribute forecasting difficulty to a challenge that applies to any forecasting method.
